data.title: Lock
data.tagline: A lock is a concurrency-control mechanism that limits simultaneous access to a shared resource.
data.learningOutcome: You can name the shared resource and lock scope, then verify ownership, waiting, release, and final state.
data.description: When two requests update one inventory record, the lock owner checks and decrements before release; the waiter then rechecks, so only one succeeds. The lock must cover the correct resource. Inconsistent acquisition order can deadlock, and an in-process lock does not automatically protect another service instance.

learning.assumes: You know requests can update the same database record or memory object concurrently.
learning.outcome: You can name the shared resource and lock scope, then verify ownership, waiting, release, and final state.

distinctions.label: Race Condition
distinctions.explanation: Race Condition is the concurrency anomaly caused by unpredictable timing; a Lock is a synchronization primitive used to prevent race conditions.

distinctions.label: Lease
distinctions.explanation: A Lock requires manual release; a Lease is a distributed lock variant with automatic expiration and renewal.

explanation.title: Problem and key mechanism
explanation.text: Both requests can read stock 1 and decrement it, causing overselling; lock the shared inventory record so one request checks and updates while the other waits and then rechecks.

explanation.title: Verify the waiter rechecks
explanation.text: Concurrent testing yields one success, one out-of-stock result, and final stock 0. Cross-instance scope and deadlock still need handling.

explanation.title: A second scenario: clinic scheduling
explanation.text: When two staff members schedule the same clinic room and time slot, the lock should cover that shared slot. After the first releases it, the waiter rechecks so two appointments cannot occupy the same slot.

data.boundary: A lock protects only the resource and scope it actually covers. Inconsistent order can deadlock, and one in-process lock does not coordinate separate service instances. Timeout and release paths also matter.

lessonPractice.title: Only one item remains and two backend instances decrement it concurrently. Which lock decision is reliable?

options.label: Use a lock that protects the same database record, then make the waiter recheck stock
options.feedback: Correct. The lock scope covers the shared resource, and a waiter evaluates the new state after acquiring it.

options.label: Create one in-process lock per instance and assume the instances now exclude each other
options.feedback: Separate in-process locks cannot see each other and do not protect one shared database record.

options.label: Let both requests decrement first, then acquire a lock to record what happened
options.feedback: The conflict has already happened; the lock must cover the check-and-update critical section.

data.agentPrompt: Lock the inventory check and update for the same shared record. Record owner, waiter, release, and timeout. Test two concurrent requests so only one succeeds and the waiter rechecks after acquiring the lock and returns out of stock. If the service has multiple instances, do not rely only on separate in-process locks.
